b: MUSKEGON, Mich. (November 24, 2026) – Back home in the Land of (sometimes frozen) 10,000 Lakes we had a name for it. Tiptoe ice. It’s that first skin of hardwater that’s just barely thick enough to hold a guy, and you walk it like you’re avoiding landmines in the Squid Game. Every step gets a little prayer, and every whack of the spud bar gets a listen.

We had a yardstick, too. A good year meant fishable ice somewhere within driving distance by Thanksgiving. Maybe a backwater slough or a little pothole lake up north, but somewhere. You’d eat turkey on Thursday and be drilling holes by Saturday, and nobody at the table thought that was strange.

This year is running a little behind schedule, however, and not just back home. A strong El Niño kept the northern tier mild through the fall, which bought the boat crowd a few bonus weeks of open water. But the switch is starting to flip. Lake of the Woods already has a veneer on the back bays, and skim ice has been forming overnight in the harbors at Leech Lake. Thanksgiving weekend looks mild, but it won’t take many cold, still nights to turn that skim into tiptoe ice.

And a later start isn’t bad news. With no snow in the forecast, whatever ice forms should come in clear and hard instead of slushy, and that’s the kind you want to stand on. Clear ice also sets up some of the best sight fishing of the whole winter.
Tiptoe Ice: Planning First Ice Starts This Thanksgiving Weekend 56
Where The Ice Is Right Now

Hardwater diehards aren’t totally shut out. A few fish are already coming through the ice in northern Manitoba, and smaller trout ponds in central and northern Saskatchewan are starting to harden. Interior Alaska usually gets rolling right about now, too, and the high-country ponds of the Rockies are close behind.

For the rest of the Ice Belt, first ice follows a pretty predictable path, north to south and small water to big. The North Dakota sloughs, northwest Minnesota and the back bays of Lake of the Woods usually lock up first, along with the parkland lakes of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The Arrowhead, northern Wisconsin and the U.P. come next, then central Minnesota and the glacial lakes of eastern South Dakota. Out East, the Adirondacks, northern Maine and Vermont’s Northeast Kingdom lead the way, while southern New England and Pennsylvania often wait until January. In the Rockies, the high-country lakes go first and the reservoirs at lower elevations follow. The lower Great Lakes states, from Iowa across to Ohio, bring up the rear. Big water like Lake Winnipeg and Green Bay always shows up late to the party.
The same goes for any single lake. Backwaters and shallow, protected bays go first. Main basins take longer, and anything with current, like necks and river mouths, is the last place to trust.
For a lot of us, the fat lady has already sung on hunting season. That leaves one thing on the brain, and it’s ice, whether the lakes are ready or not.

So, the holiday weekend comes without hardwater. Fine. Use it. Four days off is plenty of time to square away every piece of gear, every waypoint and every plan, so you’re ready the morning tiptoe ice shows up.
Tiptoe Ice: Planning First Ice Starts This Thanksgiving Weekend 57
Map It Out Over the Mashed Potatoes

While you’re digesting the heavy starches and fighting off the turkey’s tryptophan, sit down with your lake maps. That might mean an old school map and Sharpie, the computer, or the couch with your head unit hooked to a power pack and the maps right there on the screen. Either way, forget the far end of the lake. At first ice, you’re on foot, so stick to spots you can reach on foot from your access point.

Sometimes the answer is as simple as the first weed edge off the landing. Look for where the weeds break into deeper water, plus any inside turns and pockets along it. Mark the points, too. They’re a reliable first-ice spot year after year, often drawing fish along both flanks as they move along the edge. Drop your waypoints right on the unit, and when tiptoe ice materializes, you’ll walk straight to them instead of wandering around drilling blind.
Cleats and a Spud Bar, No Exceptions

Clear ice with no snow on top is about as slick as a surface gets. One bad step and you’re flat on your back with waxworms and sawdust everywhere, or worse. Ice cleats aren’t an accessory at first ice. They’re as basic as your boots.

The same goes for a spud bar. Strike the ice hard ahead of you every couple of steps as you walk out. A solid thunk means keep going. A dull thud, or the spud punching through, means turn around now. Keep testing all the way to your spot, especially around inlets, docks and weedbeds, where ice can be thinner. The general rule is 4 inches of new, clear ice to walk on, and every step until you hit it gets the spud first.
Hang a set of ice picks around your neck while you’re at it. Hopefully they’re never brandished.
And don’t go it alone. Sounds like a government PSA, but it’s true.
Tiptoe Ice: Planning First Ice Starts This Thanksgiving Weekend 58

First ice is walking ice, so everything goes on a sled you pull yourself – or no sled at all. Leave the big shelter and the kitchen sink at home. A hand or electric auger, a bucket, tackle box and rotisserie of rods is plenty. Pack light and you’ll stay willing to move.

Just don’t skimp on rods. Rig multiple combos at home, each tied for the fish you’re after. Keep light rods with small tungsten jigs and micro plastics for bluegills and crappies, and stouter versions with a contemporary lineup of spoons for walleyes, pike, bass or perch. When fish show up on the screen, you grab the right rod instead of retying with numb fingers. A rod rack or rod case on the sled keeps the lines from tangling on the walk out.

Clear first ice is a window you won’t get again all winter. Sweep away any skiff of snow, cup your hands around your eyes and look down. Green weeds mean oxygen, baitfish, critters and the fish that eat them. Brown, matted weeds are dying off, and fish leave those fast. Find the green and you’ve likely found the bite.
Work the Edges and the Holes

Sometimes fish do park in the middle of a weedbed, but getting a bait to them through all that salad is another story. That’s why every gap is worth a try. Bluegills and crappies tuck into pockets and thin spots inside the weeds, while pike and walleyes cruise the outside edge where the weeds drop into deeper water. Drill both, and drop down any opening you find. Those are the micro-spots the others often walk right past.
Tiptoe Ice: Planning First Ice Starts This Thanksgiving Weekend 59

At first ice, a lot of fish are sitting in water you’d skip in summer. Four to ten feet is often plenty, especially for bluegills, bass, and pike. Walleyes slide up onto those same weed flats and rock bars when the light goes low. If you’re drilling in 25 feet the first week, you’re likely fishing over the top of empty water, unless we’re talking about sticky bottom basins where panfish feast on teensy waterlife.
Put Your Tip-Ups to Work First

Think of tip-ups as an extra fishing buddy that goes off exploring while you stay put. Before you jig a single hole, set them along the outside weed edge with shiners or suckers, staggered across a few depths. They cover water you can’t, and they’ll tell you where the pike, and in the East the pickerel, are hanging out.

Here’s the key. Cut every hole you’ll need for the day, or first whistlestop, at once, tip-ups and jigging holes alike, then put the auger down and leave it there. Every time that auger fires up, shallow fish under clear ice hear it. Get the noise over with early, let the spot settle, and the flags will start popping while you’re jigging panfish in between.

Clear first ice is like a drum skin over shallow water. Every footstep, sled drag and auger blade carries straight down to fish sitting in eight feet of water, and with no snow on top, they can see your shadow too.

So, think stealth. Walk ninja quiet, keep the chatter down, and spread out from your buddy instead of crowding the same weed pocket. Skim holes gently. When the bite fades, don’t drill again right on top of them. Slide quietly to another hole. On first ice, fishing quietly oftentimes matters more than which lure you’re using.
Tiptoe Ice: Planning First Ice Starts This Thanksgiving Weekend 60

Walleyes and pike don’t sit still at first light and sundown. Some push up out of deeper water, and others slide right out of the weeds where they spent the day. Either way, they cruise the weed edges and points looking for an easy meal. Get ready for that invasion ahead of time. Lay out a line of holes along the outside weed edge, with a couple on the point tips and a couple out where the edge drops into deeper water.

It’s also prime time to put out tip-ups, and they don’t need to be a million miles away. Twenty or 30 feet from where you’re jigging is often plenty, right along the same edge the predators are cruising. Then let things settle and wait them out. When the predators show up, you can slide quietly from hole to hole and stay with the school instead of firing up the auger right on top of them.
And be set well before showtime. More importantly, if the show has begun, please don’t be that guy who starts drilling a puck’s throw away. I might have that puck in my pocket…

In shallow water, pull your coat over your head and watch through the hole. Seeing a bluegill flare its gills at a jig, or a crappie rise to it, teaches you more than any flasher. It also helps on fish that mouth the bait so lightly you’d never feel it. An underwater camera does the same job from a little deeper.

Lake trout country gets in on it too, from the Rockies to northern New England. At first ice, lakers often cruise shallower than anglers expect, along shoreline points and drop-offs close to shore. A white tube or a flashy spoon jigged aggressively will bring them in from a distance. It’s a short window, so take advantage while it lasts.

If some of this sounds familiar, it might be because I wrote a whole book on it. Fishing on Ice came out a while back, and copies are still floating around on Amazon and eBay. Last I looked, you could grab a used one for about five bucks, which says something about either the book’s staying power or its non-collectible status. I’ll let you decide which.
The electronics and gear have come a long way since then, but the fundamentals never die. Green weeds and quiet feet catch fish today just like they did back then.
